## Proof

**Claim:** Yes. For any isomorphism $T$ on a separable Banach space $X$, there always exists a countable dense subset $D\subseteq X$ with $T(D)=D$.

**Construction.** Since $X$ is separable, fix a countable dense subset $E=\{e_k:k\in\mathbb N\}\subseteq X$. Since $T$ is an isomorphism, it is a bijection, so the iterates $T^n$ are defined for every $n\in\mathbb Z$ (with $T^0=\mathrm{id}$, $T^{n+1}=T\circ T^n$, and $T^{-n}=(T^{-1})^n$). Define

$$D \;=\; \{\, T^n e_k : n\in\mathbb Z,\; k\in\mathbb N \,\}.$$

**$D$ is countable.** It is the image of the countable set $\mathbb Z\times\mathbb N$ under the map $(n,k)\mapsto T^n e_k$, hence countable.

**$D$ is dense in $X$.** Taking $n=0$ gives $T^0 e_k = e_k$, so $E\subseteq D$. Since $E$ is dense in $X$ and $E\subseteq D$, the closure $\overline{D}\supseteq\overline{E}=X$, hence $D$ is dense.

**$T(D)=D$.** For any element $T^n e_k\in D$,

$$T(T^n e_k)=T^{n+1}e_k\in D,$$

so $T(D)\subseteq D$. Conversely, for any $T^n e_k\in D$,

$$T^n e_k = T\!\left(T^{n-1}e_k\right),\qquad T^{n-1}e_k\in D,$$

so $D\subseteq T(D)$. Therefore $T(D)=D$.

**Remark.** Only bijectivity of $T$ (needed to define negative iterates and to get the reverse inclusion $D\subseteq T(D)$) and density of $E$ are used; boundedness of $T$ and $T^{-1}$ is not required for the argument. Thus the result holds for any bijective bounded linear operator on a separable Banach space.
